title: How to Love a Difficult Family Member
excerpt: You cannot choose your family and you cannot fix them. But you can decide how you will love them, which is a different and more possible thing.
body:
Every family has one, and if you cannot think of who it is in yours, brace yourself, because it might be you. The difficult relative. The one whose call you hesitate to answer, whose name on the holiday list makes your stomach tighten, who has a gift for finding the soft spot and pressing it. You did not choose them and you cannot trade them, and the usual advice, just cut toxic people out of your life, runs into a wall when the toxic person is your mother or your brother or your grown child. So what do you actually do? You cannot fix them. You can decide how you will love them, and love, it turns out, is a verb you control even when the feelings will not cooperate.

## Love is a decision before it is a feeling

The culture treats love as something that happens to you, a feeling you either have or lack. The Bible treats love as something you do, a way of acting toward a person whether or not the warm feeling is present. When Jesus says love your enemies (Luke 6:27), he is obviously not commanding a feeling, because you cannot command a feeling. He is commanding action, do good to those who hate you, which you can in fact choose.

This reframes the whole problem. You are not failing because you do not feel affection for a difficult relative. You are asked to act lovingly toward them, to be patient, to refuse contempt, to seek their good, and that is a decision you can make on a day you feel nothing warm at all. Start there. The feeling, if it ever comes, comes later and is not the assignment.

## Accept the person you actually have

Most of the suffering with a difficult relative comes from fighting the reality of who they are. You keep expecting the apology they are never going to give, the change they are not going to make, the version of them you wish existed. Every holiday you walk in hoping this time will be different, and every time the hope is dashed, and the dashing is its own fresh wound.

There is a strange peace in accepting the person as they actually are rather than as you wish they were. This is not approval and it is not giving up; it is realism. When you stop expecting a critical person to suddenly become warm, their criticism still stings but it no longer shocks, and the shock was half the pain. Love them as they are, not as the corrected version you keep waiting for. You may be waiting your whole life for a person who is not coming.

## Set boundaries without slamming doors

Loving a difficult person does not mean absorbing endless harm. The most loving thing is sometimes a firm boundary, a limit on the access they have to wound you. You can love someone and still decide that you will leave when the conversation turns cruel, that you will not discuss certain topics, that the visit will be two hours and not two days. Even Jesus withdrew from people, and Proverbs is full of wisdom about distance from the contentious (Proverbs 22:24-25).

A boundary is not a punishment and it is not the opposite of love. It is what lets you keep loving without being destroyed, and what sometimes, over years, invites the other person to relate to you differently. The goal of the fence is not to wall them out forever. It is to make a relationship survivable, so that some love can keep flowing across it instead of the whole thing collapsing.

## Honor without obeying, and pray honestly

If the difficult person is a parent, the command to honor (Exodus 20:12) complicates everything, because people use it to demand that you submit to harm. But honor is not the same as obedience, and it is not the same as pretending the harm did not happen. You can honor a parent, speak respectfully of them, refuse to repay their cruelty in kind, care for their genuine needs, while still maintaining boundaries and not obeying unreasonable demands. Honor is a posture of respect, not a surrender of your safety or your adulthood.

And pray for them, honestly, which at first may mean telling God exactly how hard they are before you can ask anything good for them. It is difficult to stay hard toward someone you regularly carry to God. The prayer softens you, gives you patience you did not have, and occasionally, over a long time, becomes the channel through which something in them begins to change. But even if they never change, the praying changes you, and that was a gift God meant for you all along.

## This week

Name the difficult family member, and name the one expectation of them you keep clinging to that keeps getting crushed. Set it down; love the person who actually exists, not the one you wish for. Decide on one boundary that would make the relationship survivable, and begin praying for them, honestly, this week.

You cannot fix them and you cannot trade them. But love is a verb, and that one is yours to choose.
